core: The medieval period / Middle Ages as roughly 500-1500 CE, and the point that 'medieval' is primarily a EUROPEAN periodization label coined later, not a neutral global name for the era

The 'Dark Ages' framing (Petrarch-era invention) is now rejected by historians for the early Middle Ages: the era was not one of total stagnation, and the rest of the world (the Islamic caliphates, Tang/Song China, Byzantium) was flourishing at the same time, so the age was not globally 'dark'

Feudalism in western Europe: a loose set of arrangements binding lesser lords to greater lords through land (fiefs) and privileges in return for military and personal service (vassals, lords) — a flexible system, not a rigid uniform one
The manorial system: an agricultural economy run by a lord and worked mostly by serfs (unfree peasants tied to the land) gathered into manor villages

The central role of the Christian Church and papacy in medieval western Europe (conversion, education in monasteries, legitimizing rulers, the Great Schism of 1054 splitting the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches)

The Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire as the continuation of the eastern Roman state, centered on Constantinople, Greek-speaking and Christian; Justinian (r. 527-565); it existed 330-1453 and fell when the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453
The Crusades (from the Council of Clermont, 1095, called by Pope Urban II; Jerusalem taken 1099; last Crusader stronghold Acre fell 1291) named factually as religiously-motivated military campaigns

The Black Death (c. 1347-1351): a plague pandemic (Yersinia pestis) that reached Europe from central Asia via trade routes and killed roughly 30 percent of Europe's population; Jewish communities were falsely blamed and violently persecuted
The gradual growth of towns, trade, and universities toward the period's end (High/Late Middle Ages), including the first European universities (Bologna c. 1088, Paris and Oxford in the 12th century)
supporting: The traditional end of the western Roman Empire is dated 476 CE; Charlemagne was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III in 800
Justinian codified Roman law (the Code of Justinian) and built the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople

The University of Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco (9th century) is recognized by UNESCO and Guinness World Records as the world's oldest continuously operating university, older than the European universities — an even-handed counter to a Eurocentric story of learning
The Crusades and revived Mediterranean commerce helped stimulate long-distance trade in the High Middle Ages

The Renaissance that follows the Middle Ages — owned by history:foundations:renaissance (named only, not developed)
The parallel Islamic golden age (Abbasid caliphate, al-Andalus, Islamic scholarship) — owned by history:foundations:islamic-civilizations (referenced for even-handedness, not developed)
The doctrines and histories of Christianity, Islam, and other faiths as such — owned by history:foundations:major-world-religions
Tang/Song China, medieval India, and sub-Saharan African kingdoms, named only for even-handed global comparison

claims.claim: The medieval period, or Middle Ages, is conventionally dated roughly 500-1500 CE (from about the fall of the western Roman Empire, traditionally 476, to about 1500). 'Medieval' and 'Middle Ages' are a European periodization applied later; the label describes European history and is not a neutral name for what the whole world was doing.

The old 'Dark Ages' characterization of the early Middle Ages as a time of total decline is now rejected by historians. The era saw real cultural and institutional development, and the wider world was flourishing at the same time: the Islamic kingdoms and the Byzantine Empire remained vibrant, so the period was not globally 'dark.' OpenStax frames al-Andalus and the Mediterranean's continued commercial and diplomatic ties as 'a testament to the global context of the early Middle Ages.'

In western Europe, feudalism was a collection of practices that bound lesser lords to greater lords through land (fiefs) and privileges given in return for personal and military support. It was a flexible, unequal set of arrangements that varied from place to place, not a single rigid, uniform legal system; vassals owed service to lords, and lords granted them fiefs.

Under manorialism (the manor system), agricultural production was directed by a lord and carried out mostly by serfs — unfree peasants who owed labor to the lord, lived under his authority, and were tied to the land — gathered into manor villages where their labor could be cooperative. Some laborers were free, but most in western Europe were unfree.

The Christian Church was central to medieval western Europe: it converted Germanic peoples, preserved classical learning and taught in monasteries, legitimized rulers, and was governed through the papacy centered on Rome. In the Great Schism of 1054 the western (Catholic) and eastern (Eastern Orthodox) churches formally separated after mutual excommunications between the pope's envoy and the patriarch of Constantinople.

The Byzantine Empire was the continuation of the eastern Roman Empire, centered on Constantinople, Greek-speaking and Christian. It existed from 330 to 1453 and was the longest-lasting medieval power. Under Justinian (r. 527-565) it reached a cultural height, codifying Roman law (the Code of Justinian) and building the Hagia Sophia. It ended on 29 May 1453 when the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II conquered Constantinople.

The Crusades were religiously-motivated military campaigns beginning when Pope Urban II called for a war to aid Byzantium and 'liberate Jerusalem' at the Council of Clermont in France in 1095. The First Crusade reached and captured Jerusalem in the summer of 1099. The movement spanned roughly two centuries; the last Crusader States fell when the port of Acre fell in 1291.

The Black Death reached the ports of Europe from central Asia via Silk Road caravans and Black Sea shipping in 1346-1347 and spread widely (conventionally dated c. 1347-1351 for its main sweep). It was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and killed roughly 30 percent of Europe's population — perhaps as many as twenty-four million people. Jewish communities were falsely accused of causing the plague by poisoning wells and faced widespread persecution and massacres.

Toward the end of the medieval period, towns, long-distance trade, and universities grew. The Crusades and revived Mediterranean commerce helped stimulate trade, and the first European universities appeared in the 11th and 12th centuries (Bologna about 1088, followed by Paris and Oxford). The world's oldest continuously operating university, however, is Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco, founded in the 9th century, older than the European institutions.
Charlemagne, king of the Franks, was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III in 800, reviving the idea of a Roman emperor in the West and illustrating the alliance of Frankish rulers and the Church.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact boundaries of the 'Middle Ages' and the dating of the Black Death's sweep are conventions, not single agreed dates.
positions: The Middle Ages are commonly dated c. 500-1500, anchored to the fall of the western Roman Empire (traditionally 476) at one end and to about 1500 (Renaissance, printing, European voyages) at the other; the precise endpoints vary by textbook.
OpenStax dates the plague's arrival in European ports to 1346-1347; the common shorthand 'c. 1347-1351' captures its main European sweep, but outbreaks recurred for centuries afterward.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives the period as 'roughly 500-1500 CE,' flags the endpoints as conventions, anchors the Black Death to its verified arrival (1346-1347) while using the standard 'c. 1347-1351' range for its peak, and marks approximate dates with 'c.'

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Al-Qarawiyyin (Fez) or the University of Bologna is the 'first' university depends on definition.
positions: UNESCO and Guinness World Records recognize Al-Qarawiyyin (Fez, Morocco, 9th century) as the oldest continuously operating university.
Some historians define 'university' (universitas) as a specifically medieval European institution and name Bologna and Paris as the oldest, treating Al-Qarawiyyin as a madrasa.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both views plainly rather than declaring one correct, and uses this to counter a Eurocentric account of the origins of higher learning.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft treated 'Medieval Societies' as a generic 'foundational concept in History' with no historical content — no dates, no feudalism or manorialism, no Church, no Byzantium, no Crusades, no Black Death, and no correction of the 'Dark Ages' myth.
The draft's boilerplate vocabulary and analogies said nothing specific to the Middle Ages and were discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with a substantive, date-verified account of the medieval period in Europe and its global context.
Explicitly corrected the 'Dark Ages' myth and stated that 'medieval' is a European label, noting the Islamic world and Byzantium were flourishing simultaneously.
Described feudalism as a loose, variable set of arrangements rather than a single rigid system, per the assignment and the sources.
Named the Crusades and the Black Death factually with verified dates and included the persecution of Jewish communities during the plague, handled seriously and without minimization.
Added an even-handed note that the world's oldest continuously operating university is Al-Qarawiyyin in Morocco, not a European institution.

sourceRecords.title: World History, Volume 1: to 1500 — Chapter 13, The Post-Roman West and the Crusading Movement (13.1 The Post-Roman West in the Early Middle Ages; Chapter 13 Key Terms)
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed open survey text. Section 13.1 and the Chapter 13 Key Terms support: feudalism as 'a collection of practices that bound lesser lords to greater lords through land and privileges given in return for personal and military support,' presented as a flexible set of unequal relationships that varied by place (lords, vassals, fiefs); manorialism as 'a medieval economic system of agricultural production directed by a lord and carried out by serfs or other varieties of unfree laborers,' with serfs defined as 'unfree peasants who owed labor to a feudal lord and lived under the lord's authority' and gathered into manor villages, most laborers in western Europe being unfree; the central role of the Christian Church (converting Germanic peoples, preserving classical texts, educating in monasteries, legitimizing rulers, administering through the papacy); the traditional end of the Roman Empire in 476; Charlemagne crowned emperor by Pope Leo III in 800; and the global context of the early Middle Ages, with al-Andalus multireligious and multiethnic and tied into Mediterranean commerce and diplomacy ('a testament to the global context of the early Middle Ages'), countering a 'globally dark' reading. sourceRecords.title: World History, Volume 1: to 1500 — Chapter 13 (13.3 Patriarch and Papacy: The Church and the Call to Crusade; 13.4 The Crusading Movement)
sourceRecords.notes: Sections 13.3 and 13.4 support: the Great Schism of 1054, in which the pope's envoy and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other and the eastern church became the Eastern Orthodox Church and the western half the Catholic Church, with the western church operating in Latin and elevating the pope as final authority; Pope Urban II presenting his idea of religious war in response to a Byzantine request for aid at the Council of Clermont, France, in 1095, with his directive to 'liberate Jerusalem'; the First Crusade reaching and capturing Jerusalem in the summer of 1099; the fall of the port of Acre in 1291 ending the last of the Crusader States; and the observation that the Crusades signaled the growth of the papacy's influence and 'helped to stimulate trade.' sourceRecords.title: Fatima Al-Fihri and Al-Qarawiyyin University
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry by Sikeena Karmali Ahmed. Supports: Fatima Al-Fihri (c. 800-880) is credited with founding the University of Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco in the 9th century (main mosque buildings constructed 857-859); it is 'noted as the world's oldest continuously operating university by UNESCO and Guinness World Records'; and 'the world's second oldest known university that is still operating was founded in the Italian city of Bologna 230 years later' (i.e., c. 1088). Also notes that some historians define 'university' (universitas) as a specifically Christian, European institution and name Paris and Bologna as the oldest, treating Al-Qarawiyyin as a madrasa.
